source.title: Learning Modular Exponentiation with Transformers
source.authors: D. Africa; Sara M. Kapoor; Theo Simon Sorg; Challenger Mishra

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Minor formula and text-extraction formatting issues do not obscure the relevant results.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies delayed accuracy increases on a different algorithmic task, modular exponentiation, and reports modulus-specific learning curves. This is a conceptual test of algorithmic grokking, not a reproduction of the original task or full training setup.
record.gate_note: The modulus-specific validation-accuracy jumps bear on V1. The reported sampling-method and numerical-base test accuracies do not report delayed generalization, so they are not separate rows. Embedding PCA and activation patching do not measure gradual formation of a generalizing circuit or later removal of memorizing components; they do not test V2.
record.test_reason: The paper calls abrupt per-modulus accuracy jumps 'grokking', but its setup cannot show the grokking that V1 describes. Each epoch uses 300,000 freshly generated samples, so there is no fixed training set to memorise and no overfitting phase. The paper reports no training accuracy, no comparison of train and test curves, and no sweep over training-set size. The jumps (∼20% to ∼100% for moduli 23, 46, 69 and 92 at epochs 1725–1750) are stepwise learning of subtasks under online training, a related but different construct. They are recorded under fits_no_version. Nothing in the paper bears on V2–V7: the PCA and activation-patching analyses do not track circuit formation over training, the optimizer is fixed (Adam, lr 1e-4), and there is no weight-decay, initialisation or norm manipulation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that compact Transformers learn modular exponentiation (over 80% test accuracy with reciprocal sampling) and show stepwise, modulus-specific 'grokking' with synchronised jumps for related moduli. They add that the data distribution and numerical base strongly shape learning. They also report that a final-layer attention circuit reproduces full-model accuracy on non-reduced instances.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains compact encoder–decoder Transformers on modular exponentiation with several operand and outcome sampling schemes; it does not report the original study's full recipe or a training-set-size sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: Sampling scheme affects accuracy: reciprocal operand sampling performs better than uniform operand sampling. Numerical base also affects test accuracy, with the reported composite bases outperforming the prime bases.

fits_no_version.finding: Under reciprocal-operand sampling with fresh data every epoch, validation accuracy for moduli 23, 46, 69 and 92 jumps together from ∼20% to near 100% within epochs 1725–1750. Controls 47 and 83 improve gradually. Small moduli are learned within 100 epochs; the others are learned stepwise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In online-trained Transformers on arithmetic tasks, related sub-problems (here, moduli sharing a factor) are learned in abrupt, synchronised steps with no memorisation phase. This is stepwise emergence of subtasks, distinct from grokking after overfitting.

record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2024 (as stated in the paper header); arXiv.org, 2025
record.problems: The paper does not report training accuracy alongside the modulus-specific validation curves, a training-set-size sweep, or uncertainty estimates. The jumps are reported for a compact model on synthetic data; several additional-modulus results are qualitative, and the per-modulus values are presented in a plot rather than a result table.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows retained. Sampling-method and base-comparison test accuracies do not report delayed grokking; PCA and activation-patching results do not measure the mechanism specified by V2.

untested.parts: All of it: a training-accuracy plateau before the test jump, a start at chance, a fixed small training set, and the delay growing as the training set shrinks. Online sampling precludes these.

record.verdict_notes: The key fact the reader missed: training uses 300,000 newly generated samples per epoch, so the train/test-gap definition of grokking in V1 cannot apply. I therefore reclassified the study as discussing grokking rather than testing V1, and removed the reader's V1 labels. The rows themselves are kept but linked to no version. A researcher may still find the synchronised per-modulus jumps relevant to discussions of emergence.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports validation accuracy by modulus, not training accuracy alongside test accuracy; it does not establish that training accuracy saturated first, that accuracy began at chance, or that the delay grows as the training set shrinks.

rows.operation_detail: Measured validation accuracy over training for modulus 23.
rows.note: The text reports a synchronized increase for multiples of 23; Figure 2 plots modulus 23 separately.
rows.check: Online training on fresh samples every epoch means no memorisation phase; validation accuracy alone cannot show 'generalization long after training accuracy saturates'. The ∼20% baseline is not chance (chance for mod 23 is about 4%).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Moduli 23, 46, 69, and 92 in the reciprocal-operands model
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports validation accuracy increasing from ∼20% to 100% in epochs 1725–1750 for these moduli (r1–r4). This supports a delayed, modulus-specific accuracy jump, but not the full train/test and dataset-size claims.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The controls are reported to improve gradually rather than show the same synchronized jump (r6–r7), so the abrupt pattern is not uniform across the plotted moduli.
